A course map for instructors

Source: vignettes/articles/course-map.Rmd
course-map.Rmd

This page is a suggested 12-week syllabus for an introductory course in item response theory (IRT), for graduate students in education, psychology or the health sciences. Each week lists what students should be able to do by the end of it, what to read on this site, what to run in R, and which lab and dataset to use. Take it as a starting point: drop weeks, merge them, or swap in your own readings.

Everything here runs on a laptop with mirt and mirtverse installed. No internet connection is needed once the packages are installed, and none of the examples take more than a few seconds to run.

Before the first class

Ask students to install the packages and check that a lab opens:

install.packages(c("mirt", "learnr"))
# install mirtverse as shown on the home page, then:
library(mirtverse)
list_labs()

Students who are new to R can do much of the course without writing code. The workbench (launch_workbench()) runs a full analysis by pointing and clicking and shows the R code for every step, and mv_ask() writes a script from a plain-language request. Both make good bridges to writing code by hand later in the term.

The 12 weeks at a glance

Week Topic Lab Main data
1 Measurement, scoring and classical item analysis Lab 1, first two sections certexam
2 From classical test theory to IRT: the Rasch, 2PL and 3PL models LSAT7
3 Estimation and comparing models LSAT7, SAT12
4 Dimensionality and local independence Lab 1 in class certexam
5 Item fit, person fit and item quality SAT12
6 Information, precision and reliability certexam
7 Scoring people Lab 2 in class certexam
8 Polytomous items and open-ended responses Open-ended scoring lab (coming soon) Science
9 Differential item functioning and fairness Lab 3, run_lab("fairness") numeracy, certexam
10 Linking and equating Lab 4, run_lab("linking") linking, certexam
11 Item banks, test assembly and adaptive testing Lab 5, run_lab("cat-design") catbank, certexam bank
12 Cut scores, reporting and communicating results Final project students’ own data

The glossary (coming soon) defines each term used below, and the cheat sheet (coming soon) lists the main functions by task; both work well as handouts from week 1.

Week by week

Week 1. Measurement, scoring and classical item analysis

By the end of the week, students can score multiple-choice responses against a key, compute proportion correct and item-total correlations, and read a distractor analysis.

  • Read: Getting started; “The story” and “Start a lab” in Teaching labs.
  • Run: key2binary(), itemstats() (mirt), profile_data().
  • Lab: the first two sections of Lab 1 (run_lab("model-choice")), “Score the responses” and “Screen the items”. Students meet a miskeyed item without being told it is there.
  • Data: certexam, certexam_key.
  • Discuss: what a number-correct score can and cannot tell us.

Week 2. From classical test theory to IRT

By the end of the week, students can explain the Rasch, 2PL and 3PL models, fit them with mirt(), and read an item characteristic curve.

  • Read: sections 1 to 4 of Getting started.
  • Run: mirt(), coef(mod, IRTpars = TRUE), gg_trace(), item_table(), interpret().
  • Data: LSAT7 (expand it with expand.table()).
  • Activity: ask students to sketch trace lines for items they invent (an easy item, a hard item, a flat item) and then find the closest real item in the data.

Week 3. Estimation and comparing models

By the end of the week, students can describe marginal maximum likelihood in words, recognise a model that has not converged, and compare nested models with likelihood-ratio tests and information criteria.

  • Read: “Let mirtverse pick a model” in Getting started.
  • Run: select_model(), anova(), M2(), glance_mirt(), tidy_mirt().
  • Data: LSAT7 and SAT12 (scored with key2binary()).
  • Discuss: why AIC and BIC can disagree, and what sample size has to do with fitting a 3PL.

Week 4. Dimensionality and local independence

By the end of the week, students can check whether one dimension is enough, read standardized residuals and the Q3 statistic, and tell local dependence from a second trait.

  • Run: a one- vs two-factor model with anova(), summary() for rotated loadings, residuals(mod, type = "Q3") and gg_q3().
  • Lab: all of Lab 1 (run_lab("model-choice"), about 75 minutes). It ends with a model choice the student has to justify in writing.
  • Data: certexam (the passage pair Q21 and Q22).
  • Assignment: hand in the decision table and justification from the end of Lab 1.

Week 5. Item fit, person fit and item quality

By the end of the week, students can read S-X² item fit, compare an empirical and a model-implied curve, and flag aberrant response patterns.

  • Run: itemfit() and gg_itemfit(), gg_empirical(), personfit() (mirt), item_card() and item_cards().
  • Data: SAT12.
  • Activity: students pick the three weakest items from the item cards and write one sentence each on what an item writer should change.

Week 6. Information, precision and reliability

By the end of the week, students can read item and test information curves, convert information to a standard error, and explain why reliability depends on where on the scale you look.

  • Run: gg_info(), testinfo(), marginal_rxx() and empirical_rxx() (mirt).
  • Lab: the “Precision at the pass mark” section of Lab 2 previews next week.
  • Data: certexam.

Week 7. Scoring people

By the end of the week, students can compare EAP, MAP, ML and WLE scores, explain why ML fails for perfect scores, and read a Wright map.

  • Run: fscores() (mirt), gg_scores(), gg_wright(), augment_mirt().
  • Lab: all of Lab 2 (run_lab("decisions"), about 75 minutes). Students choose a scoring method, estimate classification accuracy, look for DIF and write a memo to the board. Lab 2 fits its own model, so students who missed Lab 1 can still do it.
  • Data: certexam.
  • Assignment: the memo from the end of Lab 2.

Week 8. Polytomous items and open-ended responses

By the end of the week, students can fit the partial credit, generalized partial credit and graded response models, read category curves, and say when categories should be collapsed.

  • Read: Assessment pipeline, section “9. Scoring”, for scoring open-ended responses with score_open().
  • Run: select_model() on polytomous data, gg_trace(), gg_info().
  • Lab: open-ended scoring lab (coming soon).
  • Data: Science (four Likert-type items).
  • Students coming from ltm, eRm or TAM: mirtify() translates their old code (Coming from other IRT packages).

Week 9. Differential item functioning and fairness

By the end of the week, students can tell impact from DIF, run a DIF analysis with anchor items, and explain uniform and non-uniform DIF.

  • Run: dif(), gg_dif(), interpret() on the result; multipleGroup() and DIF() (mirt) for the model behind it.
  • Lab: the “Fairness across languages” section of Lab 2 for a short version; Lab 3 (run_lab("fairness"), about 75 minutes) for a full session, with Mantel-Haenszel, anchor purification and differential test functioning.
  • Data: numeracy (English language learners and fluent students) in Lab 3; certexam (English and French candidates) in Lab 2.
  • Discuss: what a content review panel should do with a flagged item.

Week 10. Linking and equating

By the end of the week, students can explain why two forms need a common scale, describe anchor-item and common-person designs, and link a new calibration to an existing one.

  • Read: Assessment pipeline, sections “3. Field-test design” and “6. The item bank”.
  • Run: design_field_test(), link_to_bank(); multipleGroup() with anchors and fixedCalib() (mirt).
  • Lab: Lab 4 (run_lab("linking"), about 75 minutes): separate and concurrent calibration, mean-sigma linking, anchor drift and IRT true-score equating of a pass mark.
  • Data: linking (two forms with common items) in Lab 4; certexam, split into two field-test forms by design_field_test(), for the pipeline functions.

Week 11. Item banks, test assembly and adaptive testing

By the end of the week, students can describe an item bank, assemble a form to a target information curve, and explain how a computerized adaptive test picks items and when it stops.

  • Read: Assessment pipeline, sections “6. The item bank” and “7. Forms, adaptive and multistage tests”.
  • Run: mv_bank(), assemble_forms(), simulate_cat(), assemble_mst().
  • Lab: Lab 5 (run_lab("cat-design"), about 75 minutes): bank information, a CAT by hand, simulation, exposure control, content balancing and stopping rules.
  • Data: catbank (a 180-item placement bank) in Lab 5; the certexam bank built in the pipeline article for the pipeline functions.

Week 12. Cut scores, reporting and communicating results

By the end of the week, students can describe a Bookmark standard setting, estimate classification accuracy at a cut score, and explain IRT results to someone who does not use R.

  • Read: Assessment pipeline, sections “8. Cut scores” and “11. The report”; Sharing results with a dashboard.
  • Run: item_map(), set_cuts(), mv_report(), mv_dashboard().
  • Final project: see below.

Assessment ideas

Weight Task When
20% Lab 1 decision table and model justification Week 4
20% Lab 2 memo to the board Week 7
20% Two short problem sets (one on fit and precision, one on DIF or linking) Weeks 6 and 10
40% Final project: a full analysis of a dataset of the student’s choice, handed in as an mv_report() or a dashboard plus a two-page memo Week 12

For the final project, students can follow the assessment pipeline from calibration to the report. Its flags point out what to check before each next step, which works well as a checklist for the write-up.

Adapting the course

  • A shorter course (8 weeks): combine weeks 2 and 3, and weeks 5 and 6; drop week 10 and treat week 11 as a lecture without a lab.
  • An undergraduate course: spend two weeks on week 1, use the workbench instead of code until week 4, and end at week 9.
  • A second course: add multidimensional and bifactor models (mirt() with more factors, bfactor()), response-time models (fit_rt(), sim_rt()), and the remaining stages of the assessment pipeline, such as test security and bank monitoring.
